details:
**"God is dead"**
Nietzsche's most famous declaration, which appears in nearly every question. In The Gay Science, the "Parable of the Madman" has a man with a lantern running into a marketplace crying "We have killed him," meaning that modern people no longer genuinely believe in God and have lost the foundation of their values. The idea also appears at the start of Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

**Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Also sprach Zarathustra)**
Nietzsche's philosophical novel (1883–1885) about a prophet named after Zoroaster, the Persian founder of Zoroastrianism. Zarathustra descends from his mountain cave with his animals, an eagle and a serpent coiled around its neck, to teach his doctrines, and he urges the breaking of the "old tablets" of traditional morality.

**Übermensch (Overman)**
The ideal figure proclaimed in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, a human who creates his own life-affirming values and overcomes conventional Christian morality. In the prologue, Zarathustra compares man to a rope over an abyss between beast and Übermensch, and a tightrope walker who falls to his death becomes his first companion.

**Eternal recurrence (eternal return)**
The thought experiment, first introduced in The Gay Science, in which a demon tells you that you must live your life again exactly the same way infinitely many times. Nietzsche asks whether one would curse the demon or embrace the idea; it is developed further in Zarathustra, where the thought that petty, mediocre men will also return fills Zarathustra with nausea.

**On the Genealogy of Morality (Morals)**
Nietzsche's 1887 work of three essays tracing the historical origins of moral values. He criticizes the "English psychologists" for their ahistorical accounts of morality, and the third essay asks what ascetic ideals mean for artists, philosophers, and priests, concluding that "man would rather will nothingness than not will."

**Master and slave morality**
The central contrast of the Genealogy's first essay. Master morality, of the strong and noble, distinguishes "good" from "bad," while slave morality, of the weak, distinguishes "good" from "evil." Nietzsche identifies Christianity, which praises meekness and humility, as a slave morality.

**Ressentiment, the "blond beast," and lambs and birds of prey**
Nietzsche argues that slave morality arose from ressentiment, the resentment of the powerless, led by the priestly caste, against their oppressors. He compares the weak to lambs who call the birds of prey that eat them evil, and he describes the noble "blond beast," an image of a predatory lion.

**The Birth of Tragedy**
Nietzsche's first book (1872), which explains Greek tragedy as a union of the Apollonian (order, form, dreams) and the Dionysian (frenzy, intoxication, ecstasy). It blames Socrates and Euripides for killing tragedy through rationalism, praises Wagner's music as its rebirth, and was later reissued with a self-critical preface calling the book "arrogant and rhapsodic."

**Will to power**
Nietzsche's concept that the fundamental drive of all living things is not mere survival but the urge to grow, dominate, and express strength. The Nazis distorted this idea, along with the Übermensch, for their own ideology.

**The Gay Science**
Nietzsche's 1882 book (Die fröhliche Wissenschaft) containing both the Parable of the Madman and the first statement of eternal recurrence. It also contains the passage that after the Buddha died, people showed his shadow in a cave for centuries, and that God's shadow will likewise remain in caves for millennia.

**Beyond Good and Evil**
Nietzsche's 1886 book, the prelude to the Genealogy, which calls for a new breed of "free spirit" philosophers who break with traditional morality. Its preface opens "Supposing truth is a woman—what then?" and it states, "There are no moral phenomena at all, only a moral interpretation of phenomena."

**Ecce Homo**
Nietzsche's autobiography, written in 1888 shortly before his mental collapse, with chapter titles such as "Why I Am So Wise," "Why I Am So Clever," "Why I Write Such Good Books," and "Why I Am a Destiny." It praises amor fati, the "love of fate," meaning to want nothing to be different, and asks readers, "Above all, do not mistake me for someone else."

**Wagner and The Case of Wagner**
Nietzsche was once a close friend and admirer of the composer Richard Wagner, but broke with him and later attacked him in The Case of Wagner and Nietzsche contra Wagner. He also rejected Wagner's anti-Semitism, and a Schopenhauer essay in his Untimely Meditations reflects his earlier admiration for Schopenhauer.

**Twilight of the Idols and The Antichrist**
Two 1888 works. Twilight of the Idols, subtitled "How to Philosophize with a Hammer," attacks Socrates and traditional philosophy, while The Antichrist assaults Christianity and calls for a "revaluation (transvaluation) of all values."

**Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and perspectivism**
After Nietzsche went insane in 1889, his sister Elisabeth controlled his writings and edited them to appear nationalist and anti-Semitic, assembling the unpublished notes into The Will to Power. Nietzsche's actual doctrine of perspectivism holds that there are no objective facts, only interpretations from different perspectives.
